title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Electron Applications
shortTitle: System Binary Proxy Execution: Electron Applications
summary: Electron is a framework that builds desktop applications from web technology: a Chromium engine renders the interface while a Node.js runtime executes backend logic, and many everyday chat and collaboration clients such as Signal, Slack and Teams are built on it. The abuse follows from two properties of the framework. First, Electron command-line switches that exist for legitimate graphics and launcher configuration can be pointed at an operating system interpreter, so the trusted application starts that interpreter as a child process and the resulting execution appears to descend from a known, signed product. Second, because the application's own logic is JavaScript, an adversary who can plant or modify a script file inside an installed application causes malicious JavaScript to run with the application's privileges and network access. Artefacts live at the edge of the application: process creation events where the Electron executable is the parent of a shell or scripting interpreter, abnormal launcher switches on the command line, unexpected modification of application resource files on disk, and outbound traffic from the application to destinations unrelated to its vendor. Legitimate Electron behaviour is regular in shape, so a useful detection baseline records which child processes each approved application ever creates and alerts on deviation rather than on the application itself.

beginner.definition: Electron is a building kit for desktop programs. It lets developers write an application using the same technology as websites. Programs like chat and meeting apps are built with it. Attackers can use the kit's own features to start harmful programs or run harmful script inside a trusted app.
beginner.whyItMatters: These applications are trusted, allowed, and often already open on your computer. When they start another program, it does not look alarming at first glance. Because the application also runs JavaScript, its own files can be changed to run code you never agreed to. A defender who assumes a signed chat application is always safe will miss this activity entirely.
howItWorks: The attacker looks for an installed application built with the framework, such as a chat client.
The application supports command-line switches that set a launcher program for graphics or helper tasks.
The attacker supplies those switches and points the launcher at a system interpreter with arguments.
The trusted application starts the interpreter as a child process, which then runs the attacker's command.
In the second behaviour, the attacker adds or edits a script file inside the application's folder.
The application loads its own script at startup and runs the planted code with its normal permissions.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where the front door is opened by a delivery driver everyone trusts. Residents hear the buzzer, see the familiar uniform on the camera, and open the door without thinking. One day the driver carries a toolbox that was never on the usual list and repairs nothing, but the door still opened because the uniform was genuine. The trust belonged to the driver, not to what the driver carried inside.
takeaways: A trusted application can become the parent of a suspicious child process.
Record which child processes each approved application normally creates, then alert on changes.
Treat unexpected changes to an installed application's own script files as a security event.

objectives: Describe how the Electron framework combines a browser engine with a JavaScript runtime.
Explain how application launcher switches can make a trusted application start another program.
Identify process creation telemetry that reveals an application spawning an interpreter.
Explain how planted JavaScript inside an installed application is executed at startup.
Build a simple baseline of expected child processes for approved desktop applications.
